รวมทั้งความแตกต่างของยายับยั้งการหลั่งกรดในกระเพาะอาหาร (anti- secretory drugs) แต่ละชนิดได้ 4. ระบุและจดจำกลไกการออกฤทธิ์ ผลทางเภสัชวิทยา ข้อบ่งใช้ ข้อห้ามใช้ อาการไม่พึงประสงค์ ปฏิกิริยาระหว่างยา รวมทั้งความแตกต่างของยาปกป้องผนังทางเดินอาหาร (mucoprotective drugs) แต่ละชนิดได้ ความผิดปกติของระบบทางเดินอาหารส่วนบนและยาที่ใช้ ระบบทางเดินอาหารส่วนบน (upper gastrointestinal tract, digestive tract) เริ่มตั้งแต่ ปาก หลอดอาหาร กระเพาะอาหาร จนถึงลำไส้เล็กส่วนต้น ทั้งนี้ยังอาจหมายรวมถึงอวัยวะในกระบวนการย่อย อาหาร ได้แก่ ฟัน ต่อมน้ำลาย ตับ ตับอ่อน และถุงน้ำดี ซึ่งทำหน้าที่ร่วมกันเพื่อทำให้เกิดกระบวนการย่อย สารอาหาร (digestion) และส่วนประกอบทุกชนิดที่มาพร้อมกับอาหารให้เล็กลงจนเป็นหน่วยย่อยที่ร่างกาย สามารถดูดซึม (absorption) ผ่านทางเดินอาหารส่วนล่างก่อนนำไปใช้ภายในร่างกายต่อไป โรคที่เกิดขึ้นใน ระบบทางเดินอาหารส่วนบนสามารถเกิดขึ้นได้กับทุกอวัยวะดังกล่าว แต่กลุ่มโรคสำคัญที่พบบ่อยและเป็นโรคที่ มียาซึ่งใช้ในการรักษามากมายและจำเป็นต้องรู้จักในรายวิชานี้ ได้แก่ โรคที่เกี่ยวข้องกับภาวะกรดเกินใน กระเพาะอาหาร (acid-peptic diseases หรือ acid-related diseases) เช่น โรคกระเพาะอาหาร แปรปรวน (functional dyspepsia) โรคกระเพาะอาหารอักเสบ (gastritis) โรคแผลในทางเดินอาหาร (peptic ulcers) ซึ่งอาจแบ่งเป็นแผลในกระเพาะอาหาร (gastric ulcers) และแผลในลำไส้เล็กส่วนต้น (duodenal ulcers) รวมทั้งโรคกรดไหลย้อน (gastroesophageal reflux disease, GERD) ผู้ป่วยที่มีภาวะ กรดเกินในกระเพาะอาหารแต่ไม่ได้รับการดูแลรักษาอย่างเหมาะสมอาจเกิดอาการแทรกซ้อนที่รุนแรง เช่น

เอกสารนี้จัดทำขึ้นเพื่อใช้ในการศึกษาของนักศึกษาเภสัชศาสตร์เท่านั้น 2 เลือดออกในทางเดินอาหารส่วนบน (upper gastrointestinal bleeding) ทางเดินอาหารทะลุ หรือมะเร็ง ทางเดินอาหาร เป็นต้น ยาหลักที่ใช้ในโรคที่เกี่ยวข้องกับภาวะกรดเกินในกระเพาะอาหาร ได้แก่ ยาลดกรดหรือยาต้านกรด (antacids) ยาที่ออกฤทธิ์ปกป้องผนังทางเดินอาหาร (mucoprotective drugs) และยาลดการหลั่งกรดใน กระเพาะอาหาร (anti-secretory drugs) รวมทั้งยาที่ใช้ร่วมกับยาสามกลุ่มข้างต้นเพื่อบรรเทาอาการที่เกิดขึ้น เช่น ยาขับลม (anti-flatulences) เอนไซม์ช่วยย่อย (digestive enzymes) และยาลดการไหลย้อนของกรด (anti-reflux agents) โดยการใช้ยาแต่ละชนิดมีวัตถุประสงค์เพื่อทำให้เกิดสมดุลระหว่างกรดในกระเพาะ อาหาร (aggressive factor) และกลไกปกป้องเยื่อบุทางเดินอาหาร (protective factor) ดังรูปที่ 1 รูปที่ 1 หลักการออกฤทธิ์ของยาที่ใช้ในโรคที่เกี่ยวข้องกับภาวะกรดเกินในกระเพาะอาหาร คำถามประมวลความรู้ชุดที่ 1 1. โรคกรดไหลย้อน (GERD) เกี่ยวข้องกับกรดในกระเพาะอาหารอย่างไร? 2. โรคแผลในทางเดินอาหาร (peptic ulcers) คืออะไร? 3. การลดความเป็นกรดในกระเพาะอาหารช่วยสมานแผลเลือดออกในทางเดินอาหารได้อย่างไร? 4. อาการแสดงที่สำคัญของโรคกระเพาะอาการแปรปรวน (dyspepsia) คืออะไร? ยาลดกรดในกระเพาะอาหาร ยาลดกรดในกระเพาะอาหาร (antacids หรืออาจเรียกว่า ยาต้านกรดในกระเพาะอาหาร) มีคุณสมบัติ เป็นด่างอ่อน ออกฤทธิ์โดยทำปฏิกิริยาทางเคมีโดยตรงกับกรดในกระเพาะอาหาร (acid neutralization) เพื่อ ลดความเป็นกรด เพิ่มความเป็นด่าง (ทำให้ pH ในกระเพาะอาหารสูงขึ้น) ยากลุ่มนี้ทำปฏิกิริยากับกรดแบบ ฉับพลันโดยไม่ต้องดูดซึมเข้าสู่ร่างกาย จึงมักแนะนำให้รับประทานหลังอาหารประมาณ 1 ชั่วโมง ซึ่งเป็น ช่วงเวลาที่กรดในกระเพาะอาหารหลั่งออกมามากที่สุด แต่สำหรับอาหารปวดท้องฉับพลันสามารถรับประทาน

เอกสารนี้จัดทำขึ้นเพื่อใช้ในการศึกษาของนักศึกษาเภสัชศาสตร์เท่านั้น 3 ยาได้ทันที โดยหากยาลดกรดอยู่ในรูปยาเม็ด มักแนะนำให้เคี้ยวก่อนกลืนเพื่อทำให้ยาแตกตัวและทำปฏิกิริยา กับกรดได้เร็วขึ้น ยาลดกรดสามารถแบ่งออกได้เป็นกลุ่มต่าง ๆ ตามความสามารถในการดูดซึมและความเร็วใน การทำปฏิกิริยากับกรด ซึ่งยาลดกรดที่มีจำหน่ายทั่วไปมักเป็นส่วนผสมของยาอย่างน้อย 2 ชนิด ทั้งเพื่อทำให้มี ประสิทธิภาพในการควบคุมความเป็นกรดในกระเพาะอาหารที่ดีขึ้น และเพื่อลดอาการไม่พึงประสงค์ที่อาจ เกิดขึ้นหากใช้ยาเพียงชนิดเดียว คำถามประมวลความรู้ชุดที่ 2 1. ด่างอ่อนที่เป็นส่วนประกอบสำคัญในยาลดกรดที่ดูดซึมได้มาก (absorbable) และที่ดูดซึมได้น้อย (non-absorbable) ได้แก่อะไร? 2. MaaloxTM มีตัวยาสำคัญอะไร จัดเป็นยาลดกรดประเภทใด มีความเร็วในการออกฤทธิ์ และโอกาสทำให้เกิดอาการท้องเสียมากน้อยเพียงใด? 3. การรับประทาน ONE GERDTM (วันเกิร์ด) หนึ่งช้อนโต๊ะ สามารถทำปฏิกิริยากับกรดได้กี่ mEq? 4. เหตุใดจึงไม่แนะนำให้รับประทานยาต้านแบคทีเรียกลุ่ม fluoroquinolones หรือ tetracyclines ร่วมกับ AntacilTM? 5. EnoTM มีประโยชน์ในการบรรเทาอาการที่เกิดจากกรดเกิดในกระเพาะอาหารอย่างไร? ยาขับลม เอนไซม์ช่วยย่อย และยาลดการไหลย้อนของกรด ก๊าซ (gas) หรือลม เกิดขึ้นตลอดเวลาในระบบทางเดินอาหารจากกระบวนการย่อย ก๊าซในกระเพาะ อาหารที่มากเกินไปเป็นสาเหตุของอาการปวดท้อง (gas pain) และท้องอืด (flatulence หรือ bloating) โดย นอกจากความผิดปกติในการย่อยอาหารหรือการรับประทานอาหารที่มากเกินไปแล้ว ก๊าซในทางเดินอาหารยัง อาจเกิดขึ้นจากปฎิกิริยาระหว่างกรดกับยาลดกรดอีกด้วย การใช้ยาขับลม (anti-flatulences) จึงมี วัตถุประสงค์เพื่อเร่งให้ร่างกายขับก๊าซออกมาจากทางเดินอาหารได้ง่ายขึ้น การใช้เอนไซม์ช่วยย่อย (digestive enzymes) เป็นอีกวิธีหนึ่งที่นิยมใช้เพื่อบรรเทาอาการท้องอืด โดยเฉพาะอาการท้องอืดที่มีสาเหตุจากการรับประทานอาหารมากเกินไป รวมทั้งในภาวะที่มีการหลั่งเอนไซม์ ย่อยอาหารผิดปกติ (maldigestion) โดยเอนไซม์ที่ใช้มักทำหน้าที่ย่อยโปรตีน คาร์โบไฮเดรตและไขมัน เอนไซม์ เหล่านี้ยังมีใช้ในรูปแบบความเข้มข้นสูงสำหรับใช้ในข้อบ่งใช้อื่น ๆ นอกเหนือจากการรักษาภาวะท้องอืดและ อาหารไม่ย่อย เช่น ภาวะตับอ่อนอับเสบ (pancreatitis) ซึ่งทำให้ขาดเอนไซม์ในการย่อยอาหารที่สร้างจากตับ อ่อน ยาลดการไหลย้อนของกรด (anti-reflux agents) เป็นสารประกอบที่ไม่ละลายน้ำและลอยตัวอยู่เหนือ สารคัดหลั่งและอาหารที่กำลังย่อยอยู่ในกระเพาะอาหาร เพื่อป้องกันไม่ให้ส่วนประกอบในกระเพาะอาหารซึ่งมี ความเป็นกรดสูงไหลย้อนกลับไปที่หลอดอาหารได้ ยากลุ่มนี้มักใช้ในผู้ป่วยโรคกรดไหลย้อนเป็นหลักโดยใช้ ร่วมกับยาลดกรด คำถามประมวลความรู้ชุดที่ 3 1. Air-xTM มีตัวยาสำคัญชื่ออะไร ออกฤทธิ์อย่างไร เหตุใดจึงแนะนำให้เคี้ยวยาก่อนกลืน? 2. BelcidTM มีตัวยาสำคัญกี่ชนิด อะไรบ้าง ตัวยาแต่ละชนิดออกฤทธิ์เสริมกันอย่างไร? 3. AlgyconTM มีตัวยาสำคัญกี่ชนิด อะไรบ้าง ตัวยาแต่ละชนิดออกฤทธิ์เสริมกันอย่างไร เหมือนหรือต่างกับ Gaviscon dual actionTM?

เอกสารนี้จัดทำขึ้นเพื่อใช้ในการศึกษาของนักศึกษาเภสัชศาสตร์เท่านั้น 4 4. นอกจาก simethicone แล้ว มียาที่ผลิตจากสมุนไพรชนิดใดบ้างที่ใช้เพื่อขับลม และยาเหล่านั้น ออกฤทธิ์อย่างไร? 5. ตัวยาแต่ละชนิดใน Magesto-FTM มีประโยชน์อย่างไรในผู้ที่รับประทานอาหารมากเกินไป? ยายับยั้งการหลั่งกรดในกระเพาะอาหาร ยาที่ออกฤทธิ์ยับยั้งการหลั่งกรดในกระเพาะอาหาร (anti-secretory drugs) เป็นยาหลักที่ใช้รักษาโรค ที่เกี่ยวข้องกับการหลั่งกรดในกระเพาะอาหารทุกประเภท โดยกลุ่มยาดั้งเดิมที่ใช้กันมาอย่างยาวนานจนถึง ปัจจุบัน ได้แก่ H2 antagonists (H2 blockers) ซึ่งออกฤทธิ์ยับยั้งการทำงานของฮีสตามีนที่หลั่งจาก enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cell จึงส่งผลให้ ECL กระตุ้น parietal cell ให้ทำงานและหลั่งกรดได้น้อยลง แม้ว่า H2 antagonists จะออกฤทธิ์ยับยั้งการหลั่งกรดได้ดีระดับนึง แต่ parietal cell ยังถูกกระตุ้นให้ หลั่งกรดได้ด้วยสารอื่น ๆ เช่น ฮอร์โมน gastrin และสารสื่อประสาท acetylcholine ที่หลั่งจากเส้นประสาท vagus nerve จึงมีการพัฒนายากลุ่มที่ออกฤทธิ์ยับยั้งโปรตีนที่ทำหน้าที่หลั่งกรดจาก parietal cell โดยตรงใน ขั้นตอนสุดท้าย ซึ่งโปรตีนที่เป็นเป้าหมายในการออกฤทธิ์ คือ proton pump (H+/K+ ATPase) และเรียกยา กลุ่มนี้ว่า proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) ยากลุ่มนี้ออกฤทธิ์โดยจับกับ proton pump แบบถาวร (irreversible) และทำให้ proton pump ไม่สามารถทำงานได้ โดยเมื่อถูกยับยั้งแล้ว proton pump จะไม่ สามารถทำงานได้อีกไม่ว่าจะเกิดการกระตุ้นผ่านสารใด ๆ เป็นผลให้ PPIs ยับยั้งการหลั่งกรดได้ดีกว่า H2 antagonists PPIs ยังมีข้อจำกัดทางเคมีและเภสัชวิทยาหลายประการซึ่งทำให้ไม่สามารถออกฤทธิ์ได้อย่างรวดเร็ว และมากเพียงพอในบางสภาวะ จึงมีการพัฒนายากลุ่มใหม่ที่เรียกว่า potassium-competitive acid blockers (PCABs) ซึ่งออกฤทธิ์ยับยั้งการเข้าเซลล์ของ potassium เพื่อต้านการหลั่งกรดจาก parietal cell ด้วยการที่ PCABs มีคุณสมบัติทางเคมีและเภสัชวิทยาที่แตกต่างไปจาก PPIs ทำให้สามารถออกฤทธิ์ยับยั้งการ หลั่งกรดได้เร็วและยับยั้งได้มากขึ้น กลไกการออกฤทธิ์ของยาเหล่านี้แสดงในรูปที่ 2 รูปที่ 2 กลไกการอกฤทธิ์ของยายับยั้งการหลั่งกรดในกระเพาะอาหาร (Lüllmann H, Mohr K, Hein L, Bieger D. Color atlas of pharmacology. 3rd edition. New York: Thieme; 2005.)

เอกสารนี้จัดทำขึ้นเพื่อใช้ในการศึกษาของนักศึกษาเภสัชศาสตร์เท่านั้น 5 คำถามประมวลความรู้ชุดที่ 4 1. Cimetidine และ famotidine เป็นยากลุ่มใด ยาทั้งสองชนิดมีคุณสมบัติแตกต่างกันอย่างไร? 2. Pirenzepine ซึ่งเป็น anti-cholinergics มีฤทธิ์ยับยั้งการหลั่งกรดในกระเพาะอาหารอย่างไร เหตุใดในปัจจุบันจึงไม่ใช้ยานี้รักษาโรคที่เกี่ยวข้องกับกรดในกระเพาะอาหาร? 3. PPIs จับกับ proton pump แบบถาวรด้วยพันธะเคมีชนิดใด และที่ตำแหน่งใดของ proton pump การจับแบบถาวรนี้มีประโยชน์อย่างไร? 4. เหตุใดจึงต้องใช้ PPIs ต่อเนื่อง 3-5 ครั้ง จึงจะได้ผลยับยั้งการหลั่งกรดสูงที่สุด? 5. DexilantTM เป็นยากลุ่มใด ออกฤทธิ์และมีรูปแบบยาพิเศษอย่างไร และมีข้อบ่งใช้ในโรคใด? 6. Vonoprazan มีข้อเด่นและข้อด้อยแตกต่างจาก rabeprazole อย่างไร? 7. อาการไม่พึงประสงค์ที่สำคัญของการใช้ยายับยั้งการหลั่งกรดทุกกลุ่มในระยะยาวคืออะไร และมีโอกาสเกิดขึ้นกับยากลุ่มใดมากและน้อยที่สุด? 8. Clopidogrel มีข้อบ่งใช้ในการรักษาหรือป้องกันภาวะใด และมีโอกาสเกิดปฏิกิริยากับยายับยั้ง การหลั่งกรดชนิดใดมากที่สุด อย่างไร? 9. ในการกำจัด Helicobacter pylori เหตุใดจึงต้องใช้ PPIs ร่วมกับยาต้านแบคทีเรีย? 10. เหตุใดยาลดการหลั่งกรดในกระเพาะอาหารถึงมีประโยชน์ในการป้องกันการเกิดอาการไม่พึงประ สงค์ต่อทางเดินอาหารจากยาต้านอักเสบที่ไม่ใช่สเตียรอยด์? ยาปกป้องผนังทางเดินอาหาร ยาที่ออกฤทธิ์ปกป้องผนังทางเดินอาหาร (mucoprotective drugs) แต่ละชนิดมีกลไกเฉพาะตัวที่ แตกต่างกัน แต่มักทำให้เกิดผลคล้ายคลึงกัน คือ เพิ่มกลไกของร่างกายที่ทำหน้าที่ปกป้องทางเดินอาหารเพื่อ ไม่ให้เยื่อบุทางเดินอาหารได้รับความเสียหายจากกรดที่หลั่งออกมาในกระบวนการย่อยอาหาร เช่น เพิ่มการ หลั่งเยื่อเมือกบุผนังทางเดินอาหาร (mucus) และเพิ่มการหลั่งไบคอร์บอเนต (HCO3-) เรียกรวมว่าเยื่อเมือกที่มี คุณสมบัติเป็นด่าง (alkaline mucus) เพื่อลดความเป็นกรดที่เยื่อบุผิวทางเดินอาหาร รวมทั้งยาบางชนิดอาจ ออกฤทธิ์เฉพาะที่ด้วยการเคลือบผนังเยื่อบุในทางเดินอาหารบริเวณที่เกิดแผล คำถามประมวลความรู้ชุดที่ 5 1. Sucralfate ควรรับประทานก่อนหรือหลังอาหาร และอาจทำให้เกิดอาการไม่พึงประสงค์ใด? 2. เหตุใดจึงสามารถใช้ MucostaTM เสริมฤทธิ์กับยาอื่นในการรักษาแผลในกระเพาะอาหาร? 3. Characteristics of PPIs • Physicochemical property: Acid labile (pKa = 3-5) • Pharmacokinetics – Meal alters absorption and activity – Short plasma half-life (maximum 2 hours) • Pharmacodynamics – Required activated pump for the inhibitory effect – Maximal effect is observed after 3-5 dosages Take ~30 minutes before meals and continue administration as prescribed 23 Acid + Active pumps

All members of PPIs are similar except • Dosage forms: PO and IV (acid-protective form) – Enteric-coated pellet in a capsule: Omeprazole (local made) – Enteric-coated tablet: Pariet, Controloc – Multi-unit pellet system (MUPS) tablet: Nexium – Fast disintegrating tablet (FDT): Prevacid – Dual release (DR) capsule: Dexilant • Metabolism: Mostly via CYP2C19 (genetic polymorphism) except Rabeprazole (non-enzymatic metabolism) • Drug interactions – Inhibition of CYP2C19: Omeprazole and Esomeprazole – Drug interaction with drug required acid for absorption: Itraconazole, Atazanavir, Rilpivirine, Nelfinavir, Gefitinib, Nilotinib, Erlotinib 24

Introductionto histamine and H1 antihistamines • Histamine (β-aminoethylimidazole) • Biologically active amine • Autacoids • Histamine has an important role in human health • Allergic inflammation • Immunomodulatory effects • Regulator of gastric acid secretion • Modulator of Neurotransmitter release , etc. • Antihistamine activity was first demonstrated in 1937 • More than 40 H1-antihistamines are available worldwide

Other pharmacological properties • Immediate hypersensitivity reactions – Histamine is one of the many contributing autacoids – Effects of H1 antihistamines • Edema formation and itch are effectively suppressed • Other effects are less well antagonized – Hypotension – Bronchoconstriction • Local anesthetic effect of H1 antihistamines – Promethazine is especially active – Require higher concentration than those which antagonize H1 receptor

Pharmacokinetics of H1 antihistamines • Absorption : well absorbed from GI tract • Onset : 15-30 mins • Tmax : 1-3 hrs • Duration of action • 1st generation are usually last 4-6 hrs • 2nd generation are much longer acting (12-24 hrs) • Distribution • Widely throughout the body • Peak conc. achieved rapidly in the skin and persist (≥36 hrs) even when plasma level are very low

Pharmacokinetics of H1 antihistamines (Cont.1) • Metabolism – 1st generation are metabolized by CYPs – 2nd generation • Loratadine Descarboethoxyloratadine • Terfenadine Fexofenadine • Minimal/No hepatic metabolisms – Cetirizine (active metabolite of hydroxyzine) – Fexofenadine (active metabolite of terfenadine) – Bilastine (Desloratadine) CYP3A4 CYP2D6 CYP3A4 Int J Mol Sci. 2019;20:213. Higher potency

Pharmacokinetics of H1 antihistamines (Cont.2) • Excretion – 1st generation are excreted mainly in the urine as metabolites – 2nd generation • Cetirizine, loratadine, fexofenadine are excreted mainly in the unmetabolized form – Cetirizine, loratadine are excreted primarily into the urine – Fexofenadine is excreted primarily in the feces

Enantioselectivity of Cetirizine • In binding assays, levocetirizine has demonstrated – 2-fold higher affinity for the H1receptor compared to cetirizine – Approximately 30-fold higher affinity than dextrocetirizine – Longer dissociation half-life than dextrocetirizine Biochem Pharmacol 2003;66:1123–1126
Adverse Effects of H1 antihistamines • Central Nervous System – Stimulation – Depression • Anticholinergic effects • Cardiovascular system – Postural hypotension • Others

CNS side effects of H1 antihistamines CNS Stimulation • Occasionally in Infants and young children “Paradoxical excitation” • Alkylamines (e.g. Chlorpheniramine) are more common • Normal doses – Restless – Nervous, Irritability – Hyperactivity – Insomnia • Overdose – Convulsion (particularly in infants) CNS Depression • Dizziness • ↓ Alertness Histamine Ξ H1 receptor in CNS Wakefulness Cognition Antihistamines Sedation , somnolence , hangover in the morning (Impaired cognitive and psychomotor performance with or without perceptible sedation)

CNS side effects of H1 antihistamines (Cont.) 1st Generation Drugs • Both stimulate and depress CNS • Lipophilicity • Largely cross the BBB • All can cause sedation – Strong • Diphenhydramine • Dimenhydrinate • Promethazine • Hydroxyzine • Doxepin – Less potent than others • Alkylamines e.g. CPM 2nd Generation Drugs • Lipophobicity (and are ionized at physiologic pH) • Poorly penetrate the BBB • Affinity for P-gp efflux pump • Less sedative effects – Cetirizine has mild sedating effect (Higher incidence of drowsiness than others) • Active metabolite of hydroxyzine • 30 percent propensity to occupy H1 receptor in CNS

Anticholinergic side effects of H1 antihistamines • H1 receptors have approximately 45 percent homology with Muscarinic receptors • Many 1st generation tend to inhibit Muscarinic receptors • Potent • Promethazine (Strongest) • Diphenhydramine (Clinical use) • Dimenhydrinate (Diphenhydramine + 8-Chlorotheophylline) • Doxepin • 2nd generation have no effect on Muscarinic receptors • Cetirizine has minimal anticholinergic effect
Anticholinergic side effects of H1 antihistamines(Cont.) • More common • Dry mouth • Dry eye, Mydriasis , Blurred vision • Urinary retention • Constipation • Less Common • Memory deficit

Other adverse effects of H1 antihistamines • Postural hypotension – adrenergic receptor blocking action – Especially those in the Phenothiazines • Promethazine • Rare – Weight gain – Drug allergy (Commonly from topical application) – Allergic dermatitis

Pregnancy and Lactation • Pregnancy category B – 1st generation : Chlorpheniramine, Diphenhydramine – 2nd generation : Cetirizine, Loratadine • Lactation – Antihistamines can be excreted in small amounts in breast milk – 1st generation taken by lactating mothers may cause symptoms in the nursing infant • Irritability • Drowsiness • Respiratory depression

Precautions and Contraindications • Use with caution in – Pregnant women – Narrow-angle glaucoma – Symptomatic prostatic hypertrophy • Patient should avoid activities requiring mental alertness until drug effects are realized • Drivers • Pilots • Contraindications – Hypersensitivity to Antihistamines Anticholinergic effect

Clinical Uses of H1 antihistamines • Allergic Diseases • Common cold • Motion sickness, vertigo • Appetite stimulation – Cyproheptadine has antiserotonin activity (↑ Appetite ) • Management of Parkinsonism (EPS) – Diphenhydramine has potent anticholinergic activity and can be used in management of Antipsychotic-induced Extrapyramidal symptom (EPS)

Allergic Diseases • Allergic rhinitis – Rhinorrhea, Nasal itching, Sneezing, Nasal congestion • Allergic conjunctivitis – Red eye, Eye itching • Urticaria • Other allergic reactions – Itching of Palate, Throat, Ears – Insect bite and stings • Drug allergy (Not anaphylaxis and angioedema) – Adjuvant therapy of systemic anaphylaxis and angioedema J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol. 2015;29 Suppl 3:16-32.

Allergic Diseases (Cont.) • Allergic dermatoses respond favorably to H1 antihistamines • Hydroxyzine and Cetirizine – Enter the skin readily, and sustained high conc. in skin – Well-known efficacy in symptomatic treatment of urticaria and other skin disorders • Chronic urticaria – May need high dose, particularly 2nd gen. – Combined use of H1 and H2 antagonists sometimes is effective – Doxepin is about 800 times more potent antihistamine activity than Diphenhydramineand can be effective N Engl J Med 2002;346:175-179. IBD: Pathogenesis - Pathogenesis: - Idiopathic disorder - Not autoimmune disease - Etiology - Currently considered as an inappropriate immune response to the endogenous microbiota within the intestines - Factors - Defective immune regulation - Genetic mutation - Exogenous factors Pathogenesis of Inflammatory Bowel Disease. - Normal epithelium have tight junctions and goblet-cell populations that produce peptides and mucin glycoproteins to provide a barrier against luminal agents. - Intestinal bacterial or antigen from dietary may stimulate mucosal immune system result in chromic intestinal inflammation. - Bacterial products penetrate through the mucosal barrier, then activate adaptive immune response. - Bacterial products stimulate the surface epithelium (innate immune receptor), then promote the production of cytokines and chemokines that recruit and activate mucosal immune cells. - Promote differentiation of immune cells. - Crohn’s disease: type 1 helper T cells (Th1), and Th17 - Interferon-γ, IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, IL-12, TNF-α - Ulcerative colitis: atypical type 2 helper T cells, and Th17 - IL-1, IL-6, IL-13, TNF-α - TNF-α is major contribution to inflammatory process - Promote other cell type - Macrophage - Vascular endothelium: procoagulant effects - Mucosal cells: production of matric metalloproteinase - Cellular stimulation - Production of NF-ƙB which stimulates the production of proinflammatory cytokines N Engl J Med, august 8, 2002: 347(6)

IBD: Etiology - Defective immune regulation - Genetic factors: family history is a strong predictor of IBD; more correlated in CD. - Mutation/polymorphism - NOD2 (nucleotide oligomerization binding domain2) - CD; Caucasian (<10% of cases) - Bind to intracellular bacterial peptidoglycan, and activates NF-ƙB - ATG16L1 (autophagy-related 16-like) - IRGM (immunity-related GTPase M) - Mutation of genes that shared with UC and CD - JAK2 - IL-23R (protective)-involve in Th17 maturation - Some genetic loci are associated with increasing risk of other diseases (rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis) - Exogenous factors - IBD may be triggered by microbe - Diagnosis by the presence of antibodies against them (E.coli OMP2 antibody, ASCA) - Body may react against normal flora - Antibiotics may improve the symptoms - Psychosocial factors (major lifestyle, daily stress) - Cause worsening of symptoms - Drugs - NSAIDs: disrupt the integrity of GI mucosa may promote IBD - Contraceptive: some cohort studies - Smoking - Protective effect in UC - Worsening in CD

Antiplatelets • Classified into 5 groups – COX-1 inhibitors – ADP receptor (P2Y12) antagonists – GPIIb/IIIa (integrin αIIb/βIII) antagonists – Phosphodiesterase inhibitors – Thrombin receptor (PAR-1) antagonists 11
COX-1 Inhibitors • Aspirin (ASA) – Low-dose – Specifically inhibits COX-1 • Triflusal – COX-1 inhibition is one of the possible mechanisms Wichaiyo S. Triflusal 12

Aspirin • Rapid inhibition of platelet-derived COX-1 at pre-systemic circulation • Short plasma t1/2 (15-30 mins) • But inhibit COX-1 throughout the lifespan of platelets (7-10 days) – Selective irreversible inhibition • However, 10-15% of platelets is synthesized daily – After 48 h of aspirin discontinuation, 20-30% of platelets respond to TxA2 normally – Support a daily dosing, and no need for discontinuation before most of elective surgeries 13

Pharmacodynamic effect of aspirin • Aspirin inhibits arachidonic acid-induced platelet aggregation by ~70-90% J Am Coll Cardiol. 2009;53:667–77. Maximal aggregation (Tmax) values Recovery of platelet aggregation after aspirin a single dose of 325 mg aspirin Low-dose aspirin Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A 2014;111(47):16830-5. 14

P2Y12 Antagonists • Thienopyridines – Irreversible P2Y12 inhibition • Ticlopidine • Clopidogrel • Prasugrel • Non-thienopyidines – Reversible P2Y12 inhibition • Ticagrelor • Cangrelor VASP = Vasodilator-stimulated phosphoprotein Wichaiyo S. 16

Ticlopidine • The first Thienopyridines • Inhibits ADP-induced platelet aggregation by 40-50% – Normal dosing (250 mg BID) takes 3-7 days to reach this effect • Non-linear PK – Initial half-life: 12.6 h – Long-term use leads to longer half-life (4-5 days) • Common ADRs: Nausea, Vomiting, Diarrhea • Serious ADRs (resolved with drug discontinuation) – Neutropenia – Aplastic anemia – Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) – Elevated liver enzymes 17

Clopidogrel • Inhibits ADP-induced platelet aggregation by 40-50% (same as ticlopidine) – Loading dose (300-400 mg) takes 2 h – Normal dose (75 mg OD) takes 3-7 days • CYP2C19 polymorphisms with reduced enzyme activity can attenuate drug responses – CY2C19*2 (681G→ A) – CYP2C19*3 (636G → A) • CYP2C19 inhibitors e.g. omeprazole and esomeprazole reduce antiplatelet activity • ADRs – Lower bleeding risk than aspirin – Lower blood dyscrasia than ticlopidine 18

Prasugrel • More potent and rapid than clopidogrel – Inhibit ADP-induced platelet aggregation by 70-80% • Loading dose (60 mg) takes 2 h • Significantly different effect is observed at 30 min • ADRs – Higher bleeding risk than clopidogrel – Contraindicated in patients with prior stroke or TIA or ≥ 75 yrs – Lower TTP than ticlopidine Thromb Haemost 2007; 99: 215–222. MPA = Maximal platelet aggregation 20

Ticagrelor • More potent and rapid ON/OFF effect relative to clopidogrel – Inhibit ADP-induced platelet aggregation by 80-90% • Loading dose (180 mg) takes 2 h • Significantly different effect is observed at 30 min • Non-competitive reversible P2Y12 inhibitor – Bind at allosteric site or act as inverse agonist • Also inhibit reuptake of adenosine • Metabolized by CYP3A4 & excreted via feces • Half-life: 6-8 h (active met. 8-12 h) • Unique ADR: Dysnea, dizziness, headache – Possibly related to adenosine • Bleeding risk is comparable with clopidogrel Circulation. 2009;120:2577-2585. 21

Cangrelor • ATP analogue • The only injectable drug in this group • Competitive reversible P2Y12 inhibitor • More potent and rapid ON/OFF effect compared with clopidogrel – Inhibit ADP-induced platelet aggregation by ~100% • Loading dose (30 μg/kg) takes < 5 min • Metabolized by dephosphorylation • Very short half-life: 3-9 min • Duration: 1-2 h (Benefit for bridging therapy) • Comparable bleeding risk with clopidogrel Korean J Anesthesiol 2017;70(4):379-389. 22

Ezetimibe • Dual therapy with statins prevents both the enhanced cholesterol synthesis (induced by ezetimibe) and the increase in cholesterol absorption (induced by statins), providing additive reductions in LDL-C levels • PKs – Ezetimibe is highly water insoluble – After ingestion, it is glucuronidated in the intestinal epithelium and absorbed and then enters an enterohepatic recirculation – Bile acid sequestrants inhibit its absorption – About 70% is excreted in the feces and about 10% in the urine (as a glucuronide conjugate) – No dose adjustment in mild hepatic dysfunction and all grade of renal insufficiency

Bile acid sequestering agents • Cholestyramine, Colestipol, Colesevelam – Highly positively charged molecules that are not absorbed from the intestine Bind negatively charged bile acids, then excreted in the stool Because >95% of bile acids are reabsorbed (enterohepatic circulation), interruption of this process the pool of bile acids Hepatic bile acid synthesis Hepatic cholesterol content LDL receptors (similar to statins) LDL-C levels (10-20%) Cholesterol synthesis caused by upregulation of HMG-CoA reductase Triglyceride synthesis Goodman & Gilman's: The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics, 13e.

Adverse effects and drug interactions of Bile acid sequesterants • ADRs – Drinking a slurry of powdered cholestyramine or colestipol produces a gritty sensation – GI side effects: Bloating, dyspepsia, constipation – Hypertriglyceridemia • Drug interactions – Reduces absorption of other drugs – Taken 1 h before or 3-4 h after other drugs

Fibrates • Gemfibrozil • Fenofibrate • Bezafibrate • Clofibrate • Fenofibrate is more effective than gemfibrozil at increasing HDL levels • Most fibrates have potential antithrombotic effects – Inhibition of coagulation – Enhancement of fibrinolysis Fibrates J Cancer 2018; 9(9): 1527–1537. TG clearance Liver TG synthesis J Biol Chem. 2010; 285(33): 25168–25175.

Fibrates • The drugs of choice for treating severe hypertriglyceridemia (TG > 1000 mg/dL) and the chylomicronemia syndrome – TG prevents episodes of pancreatitis • Patients with type III hyperlipoproteinemia (dysbetalipoproteinemia) – Are among the most sensitive responders to fibrates – Elevated TG and cholesterol levels are dramatically lowered • In patients with mild hypertriglyceridemia (TG < 400 mg/dL) – Fibrate treatment TG levels by up to 50% – HDL-C concentrations by about 15%

PKs of fibrates • Are absorbed rapidly and efficiently (>90%) when given with a meal • Tmax 1–4 h • More than 95% of these drugs in plasma are bound to protein, nearly exclusively to albumin • The t1/2 : 1-2 h (gemfibrozil, bezafibrate), 20 h (fenofibrate) • The fibrates are excreted predominantly as glucuronide conjugates (60%–90%) in the urine – Excretion is impaired in renal failure

Adverse effects and drug interactions of fibrates • ADRs – Common: GIs (<5%) – Myalgias – Minor increase in liver transaminases and alkaline phosphatase – Risk of gallstone • Drug interactions – Warfarin effect – Gemfibrozil and statins • Statin level (PK interaction) • Myopathy (PD interaction)

Niacin • A water-soluble B-complex vitamin that functions as a vitamin only after conversion to nicotinamide derivatives (NAD or NADP) • Only niacin itself affects lipid levels Require larger doses than are required for its vitamin effects • PKs The doses of regular (crystalline) niacin are almost completely absorbed Cmax are achieved within 30–60 min The t1/2 is 60 min, which necessitates dosing BID or TID At higher doses, a greater proportion is excreted in the urine as unchanged

Niacin • Indicated for hypertriglyceridemia and elevated LDL-C • Crystalline niacin in doses of 2–6 g/d reduces triglycerides by 35%–50% (as effectively as fibrates and statins) • The most effective agent available for increasing HDL-C (30%–40%) • Reductions of 25% in LDL-C levels are possible in high dose (Diacylglycerol acyltransferase 2) HSL = hormone sensitive lipase ATGL = adipocyte triglyceride lipase Trends Pharmacol Sci. 2011;32(12):700-7. Heart Failure • Heart failure = inadequate blood supply to the body which manifests in various symptoms from tissue hypoxia – Fatigue, weakness – Dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea – Fluid retention; peripheral edema, pitting edema • Goal of Treatment – Improve patient symptoms – Slow/reverse deterioration of myocardial function – Reduce mortality

Pathophysiology of HFrEF (Heart Failure with reduced Ejection Fraction) • HFrEF is predominantly a systolic dysfunction disorder, where the heart’s ability to contract and pump blood effectively is compromised. • The ejection fraction is reduced, typically below 40%, due to intrinsic damage to cardiomyocytes and structural remodeling of the heart. • Mechanisms in HFrEF • Myocyte Loss and Remodeling: Loss of heart muscle cells leads to an enlarged, weakened heart. • Neurohormonal Activation: Overactive nervous and hormonal systems place more stress on the heart. • Calcium Dysregulation: Abnormal calcium handling reduces the strength of heart contractions. Summary: HFrEF focuses on problems with the heart’s ability to pump, lowering blood ejection. 6

Pathophysiology of HFpEF (Heart Failure with preserved Ejection Fraction) • HFpEF is primarily characterized by diastolic dysfunction, where the left ventricle (LV) has difficulty relaxing and filling, despite preserved contractility (ejection fraction). • Mechanisms in HFpEF • Myocardial Stiffness: Increased stiffness from collagen and fibrosis accumulation. • Endothelial Dysfunction: Impaired blood vessel function makes it harder for blood to return to the heart. • Systemic Inflammation: Chronic inflammation from comorbidities (e.g., diabetes, hypertension) increases myocardial stiffness. Summary: HFpEF focuses on issues with the heart’s relaxation, reducing its ability to fill with blood effectively. 7

HFrEF (Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction) SGLT2 inhibitors help improve outcomes in HFrEF by: 1. Reducing Blood Volume and Pressure: By increasing sodium and water excretion, SGLT2 inhibitors lower blood volume and pressure, reducing heart workload. 2. Lowering Cardiac Workload: This helps the weakened heart pump more effectively, easing the burden on the heart muscle. 3. Decreasing Fibrosis in Heart Tissue: SGLT2 inhibitors help reduce fibrosis (scar tissue) in heart muscle, improving elasticity and function. 4. Reducing Inflammation: The anti-inflammatory effects help prevent further damage to the heart muscle. 5. Supporting Energy Use: SGLT2 inhibitors encourage the heart to use ketones, an efficient energy source, enhancing heart function. 6. Reducing Oxidative Stress: Lower oxidative stress reduces heart cell damage, improving heart resilience. 7. Balancing Electrolytes: By managing sodium and potassium levels, SGLT2 inhibitors reduce the risk of arrhythmias (irregular heartbeats). 14

HFpEF (Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction) SGLT2 inhibitors help improve outcomes in HFpEF by: 1. Lowering Blood Volume and Pressure: This reduces blood pressure and volume load, beneficial for a stiff heart with preserved ejection fraction. 2. Enhancing Diastolic Function: Reduced blood volume and pressure help the heart fill more effectively, improving diastolic function. 3. Reducing Inflammation and Fibrosis: This reduces stiffness in the heart muscle, supporting its ability to relax and fill with blood. 4. Decreasing Oxidative Stress: Lower oxidative stress helps prevent cellular damage, supporting healthier heart muscle. 5. Promoting Energy Efficiency: By shifting energy use toward ketones, the heart has a more efficient fuel source, beneficial for a heart struggling to relax. 15

Principles of Drug action • Stimulation: Enhancement of the level of a specific biological activity (usually already ongoing physiological process). E.g. adrenaline stimulates heart rate. • Depression: Diminution of the level of a specific biological activity (usually already ongoing physiological process). E.g. barbiturate depress the CNS. • Replacement: Replacement of the natural hormones or enzymes (any substance) which are deficient in our body. E.g. insulin for treating diabetes. • Cytotoxic action: Toxic effects on invading micro organisms or cancer cells.

Drugs act at four different levels: • Molecular: protein molecules are the immediate targets for most drugs. Action here translates into actions at the next level. • Cellular: biochemical and other components of cells participate in the process of transduction. • Tissue: the function of heart, skin, lungs, etc., is then altered. • System: the function of the cardiovascular, nervous, gastrointestinal system, etc., is then altered.

Pharmacodynamics: 1. How the drugs act on the body? 2. The mechanism of action of drug and its effects. 3. The mechanism of action represents the interaction between drug molecules and biological structures of the organism. 4. The effect represents the final results from the drug action, can be observed and measured, but not the action. 5. Site of drug action: - They can be divided into: specific and non-specific

Pharmacodynamic concepts Receptors: • Specific molecules in a biologic system with which drugs interact to produce changes in the function of the system. • Receptors must be selective in their ligand-binding characteristics, recognition site for a drug is the specific binding region of the macromolecule and has a high and selective affinity for the drug molecule. • Receptors also must be modified as a result of binding an agonist molecule. • The majority of the receptors characterized to date are proteins; a few are other macromolecules such as DNA. • The interaction of a drug with its receptor is the fundamental event that initiates the action of the drug.

Receptors that regulate membrane ion channels may directly cause the opening of an ion channel (eg, ACh at the nicotinic receptor) or modify the ion channel's response to other agents (eg, benzodiazepines at the GABA channel). • The result is a change in transmembrane electrical potential. 1. ionotropic receptors

Drug Specificity: Binding to Multiple Receptor • Many drugs bind to more than one receptor type and have effects due to activity at all those receptors. • If a drug has activity at > one receptor, that might be good --- for instance a drug that blocks both β and α receptors might be a good anti-hypertensive agent. • For instance, many beta blockers bind to both β1 and β2 receptors. These drugs can cause bronchiolar constriction at beta-2 receptors in the bronchi as well as slowing of heart rate at beta-1 receptors at the SA node in the heart. • Conversely, activity at a second receptor might be undesired— for instance a β blocker might also block serotonin receptors and cause bad dreams.

Drug-Receptor interaction • In most cases, a drug (D) binds to a receptor (R) in a reversible bimolecular reaction • Antagonists can bind to the receptor and occupy its binding site and, therefore, participate only in the first equilibrium. • Agonists, can bind, have the appropriate structural features to force the bound receptor into an active conformation (DR*). • This conformational change leads to a series of events causing a cellular response.

Drug-receptor interaction • Generally the intensity of response increases with dose • Drug receptor interaction obeys the law of mass action • E is observed effect at dose [D] of a drug • Emax is the maximal response • KD is the dissociation constant of a drug receptor complex • KD is usually equal to the dose of a drug at which half maximal response (EC50) is produced (equilibrium phase)

Assessment of Receptor Occupation Measure of Affinity • KD is a relative measure of affinity of a drug for its receptor. • KD; It varies inversely with the affinity of the drug for its receptor • High-affinity drugs have lower KD values and occupy a greater number of drug receptors than drugs with lower affinities.

Affinity & Intrinsic activity • Affinity: It is the ability of a drug to bind with receptor (just bind) – The affinity of a drug for its receptors is reflected in its potency – Drugs with high affinity can bind to their receptors when present in low concentrations and have greater potency • Intrinsic activity: It is the ability of a drug to activate a effector following receptor occupation. – The intrinsic activity of a drug is reflected in its maximal efficacy – Drugs with high intrinsic activity have high maximal efficacy because they are able to cause intense responses by causing intense receptor activation – Antagonists have no intrinsic activity. – Antagonists block the activity of the endogenous ligand by occupying the receptor and preventing the endogenous ligand binding

Graded Dose-Response Relationships: • When the response of a particular receptor-effector system is measured against increasing concentrations of a drug, the graph of the response versus the drug concentration or dose is called a “graded dose-response curve” • Plotting the same data on semilogarithmic axes usually results in a sigmoid curve, which simplifies the MATH manipulation of the dose-response data . • The Efficacy (Emax) and Potency (EC50) parameters are derived from these data. • The smaller the EC50, the greater the potency of the drug.

Efficacy and Potency • Efficacy is the maximal response produced by a drug • It depends on the number of drug-receptor complexes • Potency is a measure of how much drug is required to elicit a given response • The lower the dose required to elicit given response, the more potent the drug is • EC50: It is the dose of the drug at which it gives 50% of the maximal response • A drug with low EC50 is more potent than a drug with larger EC50

Intrinsic Activity Agonists and Partial Agonists • Intrinsic activity - The ability of a drug to activate a particular receptor when bound to it. • Endogenous ligands have full (100%) intrinsic activity. • Full agonists mimic the endogenous ligand and have full intrinsic activity. • Ex. meperidine in the previous example • Partial agonists (partial antagonist or mixed agonist- antagonists ) have less than full intrinsic activity (they are less efficacious than full agonists). • Ex. pentazocine

Intrinsic Activity: Agonists and Partial Agonists Various alkyl derivatives of trimethylammonium all stimulate muscarinic acetylcholine (ACh) receptors to cause muscle contraction in the gut, but they produce different maximal responses, even when all receptors are occupied. Partial agonists may be more or less potent than full agonists. In this case, buprenorphine (ED50 = 0.3 mg/kg) is more potent than morphine (ED50 = 1.0 mg/kg), although it cannot achieve the same maximal response as the full agonist.

Competitive (Surmountable) Antagonism • More common type of antagonist • Bind reversibly to receptors – Produce receptor blockage by competing with agonists for receptor binding • If an agonist and an antagonist have equal affinity for a receptor, it will occupied by whichever is in a higher concentration • Because binding is reversible, the inhibition that competitive antagonists cause can be surmountable by adding more agonists

Noncompetitive (Insurmountable): Antagonism • Bind irreversibly to receptors – Reduces the total number of receptors available for activation by an agonist • Because the binding of noncompetitive antagonists is irreversible, inhibition by these agents cannot be overcome, no matter how much agonist is given • Noncompetitive antagonists are rarely used therapeutically because they are irreversible • The effects of noncompetitive antagonists wear off as the receptors to which they are bound are replaced • The effects may subside in a few days

Physiologic Antagonists: • A physiologic antagonist is a drug that binds to a different receptor, producing an effect opposite to that produced by the drug it is antagonizing. • Thus it differs from a pharmacologic antagonist, which interacts with the same receptor as the drug it is inhibiting. • A common example is the antagonism of the bronchoconstrictor action of histamine (mediated at histamine receptors) by epinephrine's bronchodilator action (mediated at beta adrenoceptors).

Chemical Antagonists: • A chemical antagonist is a drug that interacts directly with the drug being antagonized to remove it or to prevent it from reaching its target. • A chemical antagonist does not depend on interaction with the agonist's receptor (although such interaction may occur). • A common example of a chemical antagonist is dimercaprol, a chelator of lead and some other toxic metals. • Pralidoxime, which combines avidly with the phosphorus in organophosphate cholinesterase inhibitors, is another type of chemical antagonist.

Quantal dose response curves • The quantal dose-effect curve plots the fraction of the population that responds to a given dose of drug as a function of the drug dose. • Similarly, the dose required to produce a particular toxic effect in 50% of animals is called the median toxic dose (TD50) If the toxic effect is death of the animal, a median lethal dose (LD50) may be experimentally defined Quantal dose-effect curves are used to generate information regarding the margin of safety (Therapeutic index)

Therapeutic Index • Drugs with a low TI should be used with caution and needs a periodic monitoring (less safe) e.g. warfarin, digoxin, theophylline • Drugs with a large TI can be used relatively safely and does not need close monitoring (highly safe) e.g. penicillin, paracetamol • Other terms used: wide safety margin, narrow safety margin

Conventional Does-response curves LD50 : Median Lethal Dose The LD50 of a compound is determined experimentally by administration of the chemical to mice or rats (orally or intraperitoneally). The midpoint of the curve representing percentage of population responding (response here is death) versus dose (log scale) represents the LD50. -The dose of drug that is lethal in 50% of the population. The LD50 values for both compounds are the same (~10 mg/kg); however, the slopes of the dose-response curves are quite different. Goodman & Gilman's: The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics, 13e Chapter 4: Drug Toxicity and Poisoning

Margin of safety VS Therapeutic Index Goodman & Gilman's: The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics, 13e Chapter 4: Drug Toxicity and Poisoning ED50 = median effective dose LD50 = median lethal dose The crosshatched area between the ED91 (10 mg/kg) and the LD9 (100 mg/kg) gives an estimate of the margin of safety Therapeutic Index (TI) a ratio that compares the drug concentration at which causes a therapeutic effect to the amount that causes death (in animal studies) or toxicity (in human studies) Drugs with a low TI must be administered with caution (e.g., the cardiac glycoside “digoxin” and cancer therapeutic agents).

Nonmonotonic Does-response curves: U-shaped Goodman & Gilman's: The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics, 13e Chapter 4: Drug Toxicity and Poisoning U-shaped dose-response curve for essential metals and vitamins At low dose, adverse effects are observed because there is a deficiency of these nutrients to maintain homeostasis. At dose that homeostasis is achieved, and the bottom of the U- shaped dose-response curve is reached. At dose that surpass to maintain homeostasis, overdose toxicity can ensue. Thus, adverse effects are seen at both low and high doses.

Nonmonotonic Does-response curves: Hockey stick-shaped Goodman & Gilman's: The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics, 13e Chapter 4: Drug Toxicity and Poisoning Hockey stick-shaped dose response curve for toxicants that are also metabolic by-products. Some toxicants, such as formaldehyde, are also metabolic by-products for which cells have detoxifying mechanisms. At very low doses of formaldehyde do not saturate the detoxifying mechanisms, alcohol dehydrogenase. When these endogenous protective mechanisms are overwhelmed, one will observe a toxic response.

Nonmonotonic Does-response curves: Inverted U-shaped Inverted U-shaped dose-response curve for ligands that downregulate their receptors. when receptor downregulation/desensitization occurs following exposure to a ligand or when negative effect occurs at the therapeutic concentration. Estrogen at high levels can have maximal effects. At supraphysiologic levels, the effects of estrogen are reduced. Endocrine-disrupting chemicals have inverted U-shaped dose-response curves. Multiphasic and U-shaped curves are common in an administered compound with multiple effects, first one effect and then another, possibly opposing, effect as the concentration increases. Goodman & Gilman's: The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics, 13e Chapter 4: Drug Toxicity and Poisoning

Pharmacokinetic VS Toxicokinetic The pharmacokinetics of a drug under circumstances that produce toxicity or excessive exposure are referred to as toxicokinetics. -How long will an asymptomatic patient need to be monitored (drug absorption and dynamics)? -How long will it take an intoxicated patient to get better (drug elimination and dynamics)? Drug Absorption Aspirin poisoning: In therapeutic dosing, aspirin reaches peak plasma concentrations in about 1 h. Aspirin overdose may cause spasm of the pyloric valve, delaying entry of the drug into the small intestine. Peak plasma salicylate concentrations from aspirin overdose may not be reached for 4–35 h after ingestion. Aspirin, enteric-coated forms, may coalesce into bezoars, reducing the effective surface area for absorption. Drug Elimination Lists some drugs to have initial symptoms develop after 4- to 6-hour of oral overdose. - Acetaminophen - Aspirin - Monoamine oxidase inhibitor - Sulfonylureas - Thyroid hormones - Valproic acid - after overdose, first-order metabolic processes for valproate appear to become saturated, and the apparent elimination t1/2 may exceed 30–45 h (normal is 14h). - Warfarin-like anticoagulants - Sustained-released formulation drugs - Drug in plastic package Drugs with anticholinergic activity, diminished GI motility, may also exhibit delayed onset of action

Type of Therapeutic Drug Toxicity •An adverse drug reaction (ADR) (อาการไม่พึงประสงค์จาการใช้ยา) •unwanted or harmful reaction experienced following •administration of a drug •administrating of combination drugs (drug-drug interaction) •Occur in normal conditions of use and is suspected to be related to the drug (not genetic). •the dose or plasma concentration has risen above the therapeutic range (typeA) •usually require the drug to be discontinued or the dose reduced. •Side-effects (อาการข้างเคียงจากการใช้ยา) •any effect caused by a drug other than the intended therapeutic effect •beneficial, neutral or harmful •Antihistamine for sedation •Opioids for diarrhea •The term ‘side-effect’ is often used interchangeably with ‘ADR’ •Side effect usually implies an effect that is less harmful •Predictable •Lack of receptor specificity •Tissue distribution of the receptor •may not even require discontinuation of therapy

Type A • ‘Predictable’ ADRs: • Predicted from pharmacological reaction and are usually dose-related • majority of ADRs in clinical practice • Can be avoided • careful selection of drug, dose etc. Types of ADRs Type B: ⚫‘Unpredictable’ ADRs: – Not associated with pharmacology of drug – not dose-dependent ⚫can be very serious ⚫May not show in clinical trials – low incidence ⚫Often involve hypersensitivity reactions

Type of Therapeutic Drug Toxicity Pharmacological Toxicity Toxic dose: - Barbiturates produce clinical effects go from anxiolysis to sedation to somnolence to coma in dose-dependent manner. - Nifedipine produced-hypotension is related to the drug concentration. - Antipsychotic can cause Tardive dyskinesia (extrapyramidal disorder), depend on duration of exposure. Therapeutic dose: Tetracyclines, sulfonamides, chlorpromazine, and nalidixic acid can produce phototoxicity in the therapeutic dose.

Type of Therapeutic Drug Toxicity Pathological Toxicity Acetaminophen is metabolized to nontoxic glucuronide and sulfate conjugates and to a highly reactive metabolite NAPQI via CYP isoforms. At a therapeutic dose of acetaminophen, NAPQI binds to nucleophilic glutathione, At acetaminophen overdose, glutathione depletion may lead to the pathological finding of hepatic necrosis due to shunting of NAPQI toward interactions with nucleophilic cellular macromolecules.

Type of Therapeutic Drug Toxicity Genotoxic Effects Ionizing radiation and many environmental chemicals are known to injure DNA and may lead to mutagenic or carcinogenic toxicities. Many of the cancer chemotherapeutic agents may be genotoxic.

Allergic reaction An allergy is an adverse reaction, mediated by the immune system. - Results from previous sensitization to a particular chemical or to one that is structurally similar. - Allergic responses have been divided into 4 categories based on the mechanism of immunological. - Anaphylactic reaction - is mediated by IgE antibodies - Cytolytic reaction - is mediated by both IgG and IgM antibodies and usually are attributed to their capacity to activate the complement system - Arthus reaction - is mediated by IgG antibody; the mechanism involves the generation of antigen-antibody complexes that subsequently fix complement. - Delayed hypersensitivity reaction - is mediated by sensitized T lymphocytes and macrophages

Type I: Anaphylactic reaction Anaphylaxis is mediated by IgE antibodies. - The Fc portion of IgE can bind to receptors on mast cells and basophils. - If the Fab portion of the antibody molecule then binds an antigen, various mediators (e.g., histamine, leukotrienes, and prostaglandins) are released and cause vasodilation, edema, and an inflammatory response. The main targets of this type of reaction are - the GI tract (food allergies) - the skin (urticaria and atopic dermatitis) - the respiratory system (rhinitis and asthma) - the vasculature (anaphylactic shock) These responses tend to occur quickly after challenge with an antigen to which has been sensitized - are termed immediate hypersensitivity reactions

Type II: Cytolytic reaction Cytolytic reaction is mediated by both IgG and IgM antibodies - capacity to activate the complement system. The major target tissues for cytolytic reactions are - the cells in the circulatory system. - penicillin-induced hemolytic anemia - quinidine-induced thrombocytopenia - sulfonamide-induced granulocytopenia. These autoimmune reactions to drugs usually subside within several months after removal of the offending agent.

Type III: Arthus reaction Arthus reaction is mediated predominantly by IgG - the mechanism involves the generation of antigen- antibody complexes that subsequently fix complement. - The complexes are deposited in the vascular endothelium, where a destructive inflammatory response called serum sickness occurs. - The clinical symptoms of serum sickness include - urticarial skin eruptions - arthralgia or arthritis - lymphadenopathy - fever - Several drugs, including commonly used antibiotics, can induce serum sickness-like reactions, cefaclor, mitomycin C. - These reactions usually last 6–12 days and then subside after the offending agent is eliminated.

Type IV: Delayed hypersensitivity reaction Delayed hypersensitivity reactions is mediated by sensitized T lymphocytes and macrophages. - The sensitized cells come in contact with antigen, an inflammatory reaction is generated by the production of - lymphokines - subsequent influx of neutrophils and macrophages. - Several drugs, including commonly used antibiotics, can induce delayed hypersensitivity reactions, sulfamethoxazole, ciprofloxacin,

Stevens-Johnson syndrome The severe skin allergic. - Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) (less than 10% of skin that effected) - Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) (more than 30% of skin that effected) Early symptoms of SJS - Fever and flu-like symptoms - A few days later, blister and peel of skin - Mucous membrane symptom occurred - Complication - Dehydration, sepsis, pneumonia, organ failure Lamotrigine, carbamazepine, allopurinol, sulfonamide, nevirapine SJS https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stevens%E2%80%93Johnson_syndrome

Idiosyncratic Reactions and Pharmacogenetic Contributions Idiosyncrasy is an abnormal reactivity to a chemical that is peculiar to a given individual - the idiosyncratic response may be extreme sensitivity to low doses or extreme insensitivity to high doses of drugs. A common mechanism is covalent drug binding to serum proteins that leads to the presentation of a foreign hapten, resulting in an immunotoxicological response.Many interindividual differences in drug responses have a pharmacogenetic basis. - black males (~10%) develop a serious hemolytic anemia when they receive primaquine as an antimalarial therapy; this development is due to a genetic deficiency of erythrocyte glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase. - Polymorphisms in NAT2 lead to a multimodal distribution of isoniazid acetylation and clearance. - Variability in the anticoagulant response to warfarin is due to polymorphisms in CYP2C9 and VKORC1 - In addition, CYP3A4 and CYP2D6 metabolize a large number of drugs in the liver.

PRINCIPLES OF TREATMENT OF POISONING - Maintain vital physiological functions - Reduce or prevent absorption and enhance elimination - Combat the toxicological effects of the poison at the effector sites The “ABCDE” mnemonic of emergency care Airway Maintain patency Breathing Maintain oxygenation and ventilation Circulation Maintain perfusion of vital organs Disability Assess for CNS dysfunction, If neurological disability is noted, check -O2 administration (check pulse oximetry) -Dextrose administration (check blood sugar) -Naloxone administration (empirical trial) -Thiamine (for adult patients receiving dextrose) Exposure Assess “toxidrome”

Toxicity testing in animal experiment •Acute exposure—exposure generally <24 h •considered to be a single exposure (or dose) •may consist of repeated exposures within a short time period. •Subacute exposure—duration is greater •from several days to 1 month in animal studies •Sub-chronic exposure—exposures repeated or spread over an intermediate time range •for animal testing, generally to be 1–3 months •Chronic exposure—exposures (repeated or continuous) over a long period of time •In animal testing: exposure ranges between 90 days to a lifetime. •Acute toxicity— •ADR that is manifested within a relatively short time •almost immediately to within several days following exposure •asphyxiation from exposure to a high concentration of carbon monoxide (CO) •Chronic toxicity— •a permanent or lasting adverse effect that is manifested after exposure to a toxicant • development of silicosis following a long-term exposure to silica

Introduction to pharmacokinetics • Pharmacokinetics (kinētikos = motion) is defined as • The movement of drug within the body • Also refer to as “what the body does to a drug” • Pharmacokinetic processes 1. Absorption 2. Distribution 3. Metabolism 4. Excretion These processes involve the passage of drug through the membrane 3
Passage of drugs across membrane barriers Adapted from: Goodman & Gilman's: The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics, 13e; 2018. 4

Passive Diffusion • Transmembrane movement of most drugs • Diffusion of drug along a concentration gradient by virtue of its solubility in the lipid bilayer – Lipid:water partition coefficient of the drug – Membrane surface area exposed to the drug • At steady state – Nonelectrolyte drugs: the concentration of the unbound drug is the same on both sides of the membrane – Ionic compounds: depends on the electrochemical gradient for the ion and on differences in pH across the membrane • Ion trapping on one side of the membrane 5

Influence of pH on drug ionization • Many drugs are weak acids or bases • Present in solution as both – Nonionized form: the lipid-soluble, diffusible – Ionized form: relatively lipid insoluble, poorly diffusible • Carboxylic acids • Amino groups • pKa = the pH at which half the drug is in its ionized form • Henderson-Hasselbalch equation 6

log (Protonated) = pKa - pH (Unprotonated) • Example: Diclofenac (weak acid, pKa 3.9) log (Protonated) = 3.9 – 7.4 (Unprotonated) (Protonated) = 10-3.5 (Unprotonated) (Unprotonated) = 103.5 (Protonated) (Physiologic pH) log (Protonated) = 3.9 – 6.4 (Unprotonated) (Protonated) = 10-2.5 (Unprotonated) (Unprotonated) = 102.5 (Protonated) (pH at inflamed tissue) (Ionized form) Henderson-Hasselbalch equation: Example calculation Adapted from: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 15e; 2021. 7

1. Drug Absorption • The movement of a drug from its site of administration into the central compartment • Bioavailability describes the fractional extent to which an administered dose of drug reaches its site of action or a biological fluid (usually the systemic circulation) – where 0 < F ≤ 1 (or 0% < F ≤ 100%) Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Pharmacology. 7e;2019. 8

Drug Absorption (Cont.) • Most drug absorption from the GI tract occurs by passive diffusion • Absorption is favored when the drug is in nonionized, more lipophilic form – Weak acids would be better absorbed from the stomach (pH 1–2) than from the upper intestine (pH 3–6) – Weak bases, vice versa • Absorption from the GI tract is governed by factors such as – Surface area for absorption (area of intestine is larger than stomach) – Blood flow to the site of absorption – Physical state of the drug (solution, suspension, or solid dosage form) – Its aqueous solubility – Drug’s concentration at the site of absorption 9

The influences of gastric emptying on drug absorption • Any factor that accelerates gastric emptying will generally increase the rate of drug absorption – Any factor that delays gastric emptying will have the opposite effect • Gastric emptying rate is influenced by numerous factors, including – The caloric content of food – Diurnal and interindividual variation – Metabolic state (rest or exercise) – Estrogen slows gastric emptying 10

The influences of dosage form on drug absorption • Enteric coating – Prevents gastric irritation – But, prevents dissolution of acid labile drug in acidic gastric contents • Controlled-release, extended-release, sustained- release, and prolonged-action – Designed to produce slow, uniform absorption of the drug for ≥ 8 h – Other potential advantages • Reduction in the frequency of administration • Maintenance of a therapeutic effect overnight • Decreased incidence and intensity of undesired effects (peaks activity) • Avoid nontherapeutic blood levels of the drug (trough concentration) 11
Absorption throughout the gastrointestinal tract Adapted from: Introduction to Drug Disposition and Pharmacokinetics; 2017. 12

Absorption of parenteral routes ROUTE AND BIOAVAILABILTY (F) ABSORPTION PATTERN SPECIAL UTILITY LIMITATIONS AND PRECAUTIONS Intravenous F = 1 by definition • Absorption circumvented • Potentially immediate effects • Suitable for large volumes and for irritating substances, or complex mixtures, when diluted • Valuable for emergency use • Permits titration of dosage • Usually required for high- molecular weight protein and peptide drugs • Increased risk of adverse effects • Must inject solutions slowly as a rule • Not suitable for oily solutions or poorly soluble substances Subcutaneous 0.75 < F < 1 • Prompt from aqueous solution • Slow and sustained from repository preparations • Suitable for some poorly soluble suspensions and for instillation of slow-release implants • Appropriate for self- administration (e.g., insulin) • Not suitable for large volumes • Possible pain or necrosis from irritating substances Intramuscular 0.75 < F < 1 • Prompt from aqueous solution • Slow and sustained from repository preparations • Suitable for moderate volumes, oily vehicles, and some irritating substances • Precluded during anticoagulant therapy • May interfere with interpretation of certain diagnostic tests (e.g., creatine kinase) Oral ingestion .05 < F < 1 • Variable, depends on many factors • Most convenient and economical; usually safer • Requires patient compliance • Bioavailability potentially erratic and incomplete Goodman & Gilman's: The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics, 13e; 2018. 13

Other routes of administration • Pulmonary Absorption – Gaseous and volatile drugs may be inhaled and absorbed through the pulmonary epithelium and mucous membranes of the respiratory tract – Access to the circulation is rapid because the lung’s surface area is large – Advantages are: the almost instantaneous absorption of a drug into the blood, avoidance of first-pass loss, local application of the drug at the desired site • Topical Application – Mucous Membranes, Eye – Skin: Transdermal Absorption • Absorption is dependent on the surface area and lipid solubility Goodman & Gilman's: The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics, 13e; 2018. 10-20% 80-90% First-pass metabolism 14

The influences of protein binding on drug distribution • Many drugs circulate in the bloodstream bound to plasma proteins – The binding is usually reversible – Albumin binds acidic drugs; 1-acid glycoprotein binds basic drugs – Others: hormone carrier proteins, e.g. sex hormone–binding globulin • Binding to plasma proteins limits – Drug concentration at its site of action because only unbound drug is in equilibrium across membranes – Drug’s glomerular filtration, drug transport and metabolism • Competition for plasma protein-binding may cause one drug to elevate the concentration of one bound less avidly 16

Volume of distribution • Volume of distribution (Vd) is an important indicator of the extent of drug distribution into body fluids and tissues 1Concepts in Clinical Pharmacokinetics, 6th ed; 2014, 2Pharmacology and Therapeutics for Dentistry, 7th ed; 2017. In 70 kg male; 17

Drug accumulation • Many drugs accumulate in tissues at higher concentrations • Tissue binding of drugs usually occurs with cellular constituents such as proteins, phospholipids, or nuclear proteins – Generally is reversible • May serve as a reservoir that prolongs drug action in that same tissue or at a distant site reached through the circulation – e.g., macrolides and respiratory fluoroquinolone antibiotics • Tissue binding and accumulation also can produce local toxicity – e.g., renal and ototoxicity associated with aminoglycoside antibiotics 19

Drug accumulation (Cont.) • Bone – The tetracycline antibiotics (and other divalent metal-ion chelating agents) and heavy metals – May accumulate in bone by adsorption onto the bone crystal surface and eventual incorporation into the crystal lattice • Fat – May serve as a reservoir for lipid-soluble drugs – In obese persons, the fat content of the body may be as high as 50% M Dent J 2014;34(1):55-69. 20

Drug redistribution • IV anesthetic thiopental, a lipid-soluble drug • Because blood flow to the brain is high and thiopental readily crosses the BBB – Reaches maximal concentration in brain rapidly • Subsequently, the plasma and brain concentrations decrease as thiopental redistributes to other tissues, such as muscle and, finally, adipose tissue • QUICK ON-OFF Goodman & Gilman's: The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics, 13e; 2018. 21

4. Excretion of Drugs • Drugs are eliminated from the body either unchanged or as metabolites 1) The kidney is the most important organ for excreting drugs and their metabolites – Renal excretion of unchanged drug is a major route of elimination for 25%–30% of drugs administered to humans – During adulthood, there is a slow decline in renal function, about 1% per year 2) Biliary and fecal excretion 3) Other minor routes: Lung, breast milk, sweat, saliva, tear 27

Renal Excretion Three distinct processes: 1) Glomerular filtration – Glomerular filtration rate – Extent of protein binding 2) Active tubular secretion 3) Passive tubular reabsorption – Nonionized forms of weak acids and bases – When urine is made more alkaline, weak acids are largely ionized and are excreted more rapidly and to a greater extent; – Effects of changing urine pH are opposite for weak bases • Renal impairment may lead to a reduction in drug excretion – Serum creatinine (Scr) – Creatinine clearance (CrCl) or eGFR Goodman & Gilman's: The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics, 13e; 2018. 28

Biliary and Fecal Excretion • Drugs and metabolites present in bile are released into the GI tract • The drugs and metabolites can be reabsorbed into the body from the intestine called “enterohepatic recycling” – Conjugated metabolites such as glucuronides, may require enzymatic hydrolysis by the intestinal microflora – May prolong significantly the presence of a drug (or toxin) and its effects within the body • Biliary excretions and unabsorbed drug are excreted in the feces Adapted from: AANA J. 2020;88(1):71-6. 29

Understanding pharmacokinetic parameters • Cp = Plasma concentration • MEC = Minimum effective concentration • MTC = Minimum toxic concentration MTC MTC Goodman & Gilman's: The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics, 13e; 2018. 30

Understanding pharmacokinetic parameters (Cont.1) Parameter Name Significance Key features Cmax Maximum plasma concentration The highest drug concentration observed in plasma following administration Cmax and Tmax are correlated and both depend on how quickly the drug enters into and is eliminated from the body Tmax Time until Cmax is reached The time at which the highest drug concentration occurs AUC Area under the concentration - time curve The measure of the total systemic exposure to the drug It represents the amount of unchanged drug that has reached the general circulation and it is useful to define the bioavailability of a drug Vd Volume of distribution The apparent volume into which the drug is dissolved It depends on binding to plasma proteins and tissues and it is useful to correlate the drug concentration in plasma with its amount in the body t1/2 Half-life in the terminal phase The time taken for the plasma concentration to fall by one half once distribution equilibrium has been achieved It is independent of the amount of drug in the body and it is useful for the determination of the frequency of drug administration Cl Clearance The rate of drug elimination by all routes normalized to the concentration of the drug It is the sum of all organs clearance, especially hepatic and renal clearance Mass Spectrom Rev. 2017;36(2):213-51. 31
Understanding pharmacokinetic parameters (Cont.2) Goodman & Gilman's: The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics, 13e; 2018. 32

Understanding pharmacokinetic parameters (Cont.3) Steady-state concentration (Css) is defined as the time during which the concentration remains stable or consistent when the drug is given repeatedly or continuously (IV infusion) Goodman & Gilman's: The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics, 13e; 2018. 33

Other terms in pharmacokinetics • First-order kinetics – For most drugs in their therapeutic concentration ranges – “The fraction of drug removed by metabolism is constant” – The amount of drug metabolized per unit time is proportional to the plasma concentration of the drug (Cp) • Zero-order kinetics – For some drugs, such as ethanol, phenytoin and voriconazole – “A constant amount of drug is metabolized per unit time” – Metabolic capacity is saturated at the concentrations employed – Zero-order kinetics can also occur at high (toxic) concentrations as drug-metabolizing capacity becomes saturated 34

Other terms in pharmacokinetics (Cont.) • Bioequivalence – Generic (local made) versus brand name (original) – Drug products are considered to be pharmaceutical equivalent if they contain the same active ingredients and are identical in strength or concentration, dosage form, and route of administration – Two pharmaceutically equivalent drug products are considered to be bioequivalent when the rates and extents of bioavailability of the active ingredient in the two products are not significantly different under suitable and identical test conditions – Courts have not always found generic and brand name drugs to be legally equivalent 35

CLO1 : อธิบายหลักการทั่วไปในการออกฤทธิ์ของยา เภสัชจลนศาสตร์ เภสัชพันธุศาสตร์ หลักการเกิดพิษและการเกิดอาการ ไม่พึงประสงค์จากการใช้ยา รวมทั้งปฏิกิริยาระหว่างยา 2. CLO2 : อธิบายกลไกการออกฤทธิ์ ฤทธิ์ทางเภสัชวิทยา ข้อบ่งใช้ อาการไม่พึงประสงค์ ปฏิกิริยาระหว่างยา ข้อควรระวังและข้อ ห้ามใช้ รวมทั้งการเลือกใช้ยาอย่างเหมาะสมบนพื้นฐานความรู้ทางเภสัชวิทยาของยากลุ่มที่ออกฤทธิ์ต่อระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติ ยาที่ใช้รักษาโรคเกี่ยวกับทางเดินอาหาร ยาต้านอักเสบ ออตาคอยด์และยาต้านออตาคอยด์ ยาขับปัสสาวะ ยาขยายหลอดเลือด ยาที่ใช้รักษาโรคหัวใจและหลอดเลือด (เช่น ภาวะความดันโลหิตสูง โรคหัวใจเต้นผิดจังหวะ ภาวะปวดเค้นหัวใจ โรคหัวใจ ล้มเหลว) ยาลดระดับไขมันในเลือด ยาต้านเกล็ดเลือด ยาต้านการแข็งตัวของเลือดและยาสลายลิ่มเลือด 3.
